sections.d: อ่านบทความวิชาการแล้วตอบคำถาม 9 ข้อ

p.t: How Numbers Came to Be Written
x: The earliest written signs that survive from Mesopotamia are not names or prayers but quantities. Small clay tokens shaped as cones, spheres and discs appear at village sites from about 8000 BC, and each shape seems to have stood for a measure of grain, oil or livestock. For thousands of years the tokens were used loose, presumably counted out and handed over with a delivery. Around 3400 BC, in the growing cities of the south, accountants began sealing tokens inside hollow clay balls so that the contents of a shipment could not be altered in transit.

The sealed ball created an obvious inconvenience: no one could check the count without breaking the container. The solution was to press the tokens into the wet surface of the ball before sealing it, leaving a set of impressions that recorded what was inside. Once the impressions existed, the tokens themselves became unnecessary, and within a few generations the ball had flattened into a tablet carrying marks alone. This sequence is one of the few cases in which the birth of a writing system can be followed step by step in the archaeological record.

An unexpected feature of the earliest tablets is that the signs were not yet abstract numbers. A sign meaning 'three' did not exist; instead there were separate signs for three jars of oil and three baskets of grain, because the counting systems for different commodities were different. Grain was counted in units that grouped by tens and sixes, while other goods used other groupings. Abstract number signs, which could be attached to any commodity, appear only later, and their arrival is visible in the tablets as a sudden simplification: the number of distinct signs falls sharply while the range of things that can be recorded grows.

Historians disagree about what drove the change. One view emphasises administrative pressure, arguing that as temple estates grew, scribes handling many commodities had a practical need for a single set of numerals. A second view stresses schooling: once scribes were trained in one place, a common notation would spread whether or not any individual official demanded it. The two explanations are not incompatible, and the evidence — lists of signs that look like teaching exercises, found alongside genuine accounts — has been used to support both.

sections.d: อ่านบทความวิชาการแล้วตอบคำถาม 9 ข้อ

x: Every year the world's deserts release somewhere between one and two billion tonnes of fine mineral particles into the atmosphere. The largest single source is the Bodélé Depression in Chad, the dried floor of a lake that once covered an area the size of a small sea. Its sediments are made largely of the skeletons of microscopic freshwater algae, which are light, brittle and easily lifted. A corridor between two mountain ranges funnels wind across the depression, and on a windy winter morning the plume can be seen from orbit stretching westwards for a thousand kilometres.

Once airborne, dust does not behave like a simple pollutant. Particles scatter incoming sunlight, which cools the surface beneath them, but they also absorb heat, which warms the layer of air in which they float. The net effect on temperature depends on the colour of the particles, the height at which they travel and the brightness of the land or ocean below. Regional climate models that omit dust reproduce the seasonal rainfall of West Africa poorly, but adding it does not simply improve the result; it shifts the errors somewhere else, which is why the topic remains uncomfortable for modellers.

The most celebrated consequence of desert dust lies far from any desert. Saharan particles crossing the Atlantic carry phosphorus and iron, nutrients that are scarce in the weathered soils of the Amazon basin, and measurements of dust deposition suggest that the supply is enough to matter for forest growth. The same dust, however, arrives on Caribbean reefs, where nutrients are not welcome and where dust-borne bacteria and fungi have been suspected of contributing to coral disease. A single physical process is therefore beneficial in one ecosystem and possibly damaging in another a few hundred kilometres away.

Whether dust emission will increase as the climate warms is unresolved. Warming and drying might expose more bare ground, but a warmer atmosphere also holds more moisture and may increase vegetation in some semi-arid regions, which stabilises soil. Records from ice cores show that during the last glacial period the atmosphere carried several times as much dust as it does today, which tells us that cold, dry climates can be very dusty indeed; it does not tell us what a hot, unevenly wet world will do.

items.q: Why is the same dust a problem for Caribbean reefs?
c: Nutrients are unwelcome there and dust may carry disease organisms.
It buries the corals under a layer of sediment.
It lowers the temperature of the water too far.
It blocks the light that corals need entirely.

items.q: What point does the writer make by comparing the Amazon and the reefs?
c: That dust travels further than expected.
That one physical process can help one ecosystem and harm another.
That reefs and forests need the same nutrients.
That dust deposition cannot be measured accurately.
